items.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002
items.q: in that period we remained close personal friends. And we saw a lot of each other, we talked to each other a lot, we shared non-musical things

ctx.x: period of working together. Because the circumstances change. I mean you don’t have that regularity because practically you’re always either planning or doing or coming off of a record date when you’re working together. And there’s a great deal of planning together and hanging out together. And when that goes, what you have to recognize is you’re not going to have in most cases, that same kind of closeness. And you have to realize nobody’s mad at anybody necessarily. Sometimes yes, but very often not, it’s just…

Cannonball, who was coming near the end of his Capitol contract and Capitol wasn’t doing anything in jazz at that point. And so Cannonball and I ended up together at Fantasy for what turned out to be the last few years of his life. But in that intervening period between 1964 when Riverside died, and 1973 when we both were together at Fantasy, in that period we remained close personal friends. And we saw a lot of each other, we talked to each other a lot, we shared non-musical things, and that I have to say is…

items.title: Orrin Keepnews — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: We signed Cannonball, and part of the deal, a very important part of the deal, is his feeling that if he had had any kind of label support he could have kept this band together.

ctx.x: bothering to tell me about it, had made two changes in the band. One of them was actually there before I got there. The only time we could get, we were working at Reeves, was late morning into early afternoon kind of thing. I think we had like a ten-o-clock start. I get there, and one of the people was already there, but he was fast asleep on the floor on the studio. That was a young bass player, who had recently started working for Miles Davis. Having had a fight with Oscar Pettiford during the previous session.…

contract that he had signed, and it wasn’t Savoy it was Mercury; it was Mercury. They did a couple of albums, but the first…They did an album by, supposedly, the working group. That came out shortly after Cannonball had broken up that band, because it wasn’t doing anything, it wasn’t getting anything. So, at any rate, that led to the Adderely’s signing with us. Cannonball was the first artist I ever worked with who had a manager. So, I remember this meeting involving Cannonball, Grauer, myself, and John Levy, who…
We’re going to run out of time. I’m looking up there at all your Grammy awards and we should probably talk about, since some of them were received in the last ten or fifteen years--
